title: Why You Don’t Have To Be Perfect For Good Classroom Management
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Reflecting on his own first year of teaching, Linsin credits his early success not to mastery of any elaborate system but to two simple commitments, learned from watching a formative high school teacher and from summers working with kids: making students genuinely love being in class through storytelling, humor, warmth, and personal interest in them, and holding them accountable for disrupting class through a clear, visible set of rules with consistent consequences communicated to both students and parents. He is candid that at the time he didn't know the curriculum well and had none of the strategies he would later develop into SCM, yet the class was well-behaved and full of engagement anyway. He draws the explicit lesson that new teachers need not memorize every strategy or achieve perfection to have a successful year — getting these two fundamentals right creates a strong foundation onto which further skills can be layered gradually over time.
points: The author credits his own successful first year of teaching to just two commitments, not mastery of any elaborate system.
The first was making students genuinely love being in class through storytelling, humor, warmth, and personal interest, without special games or tricks.
The second was holding students accountable for disrupting class via clear rules, one warning, and a couple of time-out desks, communicated to parents in advance.
He credits a formative high school English teacher, Bill Heyde, as the role model whose example shaped these two commitments.
The explicit lesson is that new teachers don't need to memorize every SCM strategy or achieve perfection — getting these two fundamentals right is enough for a successful year.
quotes: All four years of high school I took a class from an English teacher named Bill Heyde , who through his example showed me what good teaching and effective classroom management looked like.
And second, I focused on two things at the exclusion of nearly everything else.
The first is that I did everything I could to make my students love school .
The second thing I did was hold them accountable for disrupting the class. I made a rough poster out of construction paper where I listed a set of basic rules .
And it worked. It worked really well. The kids indeed loved being in the class and were remarkably well behaved.
You just have to make sure you get these two things right. The rest you can learn and add to your game as time goes on.
